You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Apple Q3 Revenue Slightly Beats Expectations, iPhone Up 22% but Services and China Disappoint; Supply Shortages Weigh on Guidance, Shares Fall Over 6% After Hours

TEXT:
Core Viewpoint
Apple reported fiscal third-quarter 2026 results (ended June 27), with total revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% year over year, slightly above market expectations. Diluted EPS came in at $2.02, up 29% year over year and appearing to beat estimates, but the beat was largely driven by a one- time $0.11 benefit from U.S. tariff refunds. iPhone revenue grew 22% and Mac significantly exceeded expectations, serving as the main highlights. However, Services came in below expectations, Greater China growth slowed, and iPad clearly missed. The company’s fiscal fourth-quarter revenue growth guidance of 9%–11% fell short of market expectations, with management explicitly warning that component supply shortages would weigh on hardware. Shares fell more than 6% in after-hours trading. Investors are increasingly concerned about the quality of Services growth, the sustainability of China demand, and ongoing supply-chain pressures.
Detailed Breakdown
1. Overall Revenue and Profit Performance
Quarterly revenue: $109.4 billion, up approximately 16% year over year, slightly above market expectations (around $108.65–$108.8 billion).
Diluted EPS: $2.02, up 29% year over year, above the consensus estimate of roughly $1.89. This included a one-time $0.11 benefit from tariff refunds; excluding the benefit, EPS was approximately $1.91 and still modestly above expectations.
Gross margin: 50.1%, including an approximately 2-percentage-point favorable impact from tariff refunds.
Operating cash flow reached a June-quarter record; the company declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share.
While EPS and cash flow set June-quarter records, the quality of the beat was questioned due to the one-time tariff benefit, raising investor concerns about earnings sustainability.
2. Product Business Performance
iPhone: $54.25 billion, up approximately 22% year over year, slightly above expectations. It accounted for nearly half of total revenue and set a June-quarter record, stabilizing the core business.
Mac: $10.35 billion, up approximately 29% year over year, significantly above expectations by about 20%. This was the biggest positive surprise of the quarter.
iPad: $6.19 billion, clearly below expectations by roughly 10% and down year over year, reflecting ongoing demand and upgrade-cycle challenges.
Wearables, Home and Accessories: $7.88 billion, largely in line with expectations.
Overall product revenue exceeded expectations, primarily driven by iPhone and Mac, though performance was uneven across categories.
3. Services Business and Regional Performance
Services revenue: $30.74 billion, up 12% year over year, approximately 2% below expectations and slightly down sequentially, ending a multi-quarter streak of sequential records. As a high-margin business, the miss carries greater weight for long-term valuation.
Greater China: $18.82 billion, up 22% year over year. Growth slowed and came in below expectations, reigniting concerns about iPhone demand, local competition, and the sustainability of the recovery.
All other geographic segments delivered double-digit growth, with overall regional performance remaining solid.
CEO Tim Cook described the quarter as the company’s strongest June quarter ever, with double-digit revenue growth across iPhone, Mac, Services, and every geographic segment.
4. Cash Flow and Shareholder Returns
Operating cash flow set a June-quarter record, underscoring continued strong cash-generation capability.
The board declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share, maintaining shareholder returns.
The company did not raise large-scale capital expenditure guidance, but explicitly noted that shortages of components such as memory chips would affect upcoming hardware shipments.
5. Next Quarter Guidance (Fiscal 2026 Fourth Quarter)
Expected year-over-year revenue growth: 9%–11%, below the market consensus of approximately 12.1%.
Component supply constraints are expected to impact iPhone, Mac, and iPad, with foreign-exchange fluctuations also acting as a headwind.
Management described the supply constraints as “very significant,” with limited flexibility in the supply chain, and said the company is evaluating alternative options.
6. Market Background and Investor Concerns
Core tension: Hardware (especially iPhone and Mac) performed strongly, but the Services miss, slower China growth, supply shortages, and softer guidance raised questions about growth quality and sustainability.
Investor reaction: Shares fell about 6% in after-hours trading as the market focused on the one-time nature of the EPS beat, the Services shortfall, and supply-chain warnings.
Analyst perspective: Hardware strength may not fully carry into the next quarter. Investors are looking for clearer progress on AI product commercialization and signs of a more durable China recovery. Once the tariff refund benefit fades, earnings quality will become a key focus.
